evidence.label: Weak pure infiniteness and O-infinity absorption

headline: Proves that pure infiniteness implies strong pure infiniteness for every C*-algebra, answering part of a Kirchberg–Rørdam question.
scope: All complex C*-algebras, including nonunital and nonseparable ones; the fixed-amplification result is for exact algebras, and O∞ absorption for separable nuclear ones.
plain: In some operator algebras, an element can hold two full copies of itself, like an infinite hotel that houses two groups of guests. Kirchberg and Rørdam defined weak, ordinary and strong versions of this property and asked whether they agree. This paper proves ordinary implies strong for every C*-algebra, and that weak implies ordinary for exact algebras. Lean checks both results. For separable nuclear algebras, it follows that they absorb the Cuntz algebra O∞.
doesNot: This does not show that weak pure infiniteness implies ordinary pure infiniteness for algebras that are not exact.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Kirchberg and Rørdam, who introduced weak and strong pure infiniteness and posed Question 9.5
scorecard.significanceWhy: It answers the ordinary-to-strong part of a Kirchberg–Rørdam question in general, and the full question for exact algebras, with Lean checks.

explanation:
Take the space of infinite sequences with basis vectors e0, e1, e2, and so on. Let S1 send e_n to e_(2n) and S2 send e_n to e_(2n+1). So S1 sends e3 to e6, and S2 sends e3 to e7. Each map keeps lengths. S1 fills the even slots and S2 fills the odd slots, with no overlap. So the identity holds two full copies of itself side by side. Matrices cannot do this: two copies of the k-by-k identity have trace 2k, more than k.

A C*-algebra is a family of operators closed under sums, products, adjoints and limits. A positive element h is properly infinite when h ⊕ h fits below h in the sense of Cuntz comparison[5]. Cuntz comparison means h ⊕ h can be squeezed into h by operators, up to small errors. Pure infiniteness asks this for every positive element. Weak pure infiniteness asks it only after taking n copies of each element, for one fixed n. Strong pure infiniteness also requires two elements to be cut apart at once, with their mixed entry made small[6]. Strong implies ordinary, and ordinary implies weak. Kirchberg and Rørdam asked whether the reverse implications hold[7]. The obstacle is the mixed entry. Knowing each element alone is infinite says nothing direct about how two elements interact.

The paper proves that if every positive element is properly infinite, the algebra is strongly purely infinite[1]. It needs no exactness, nuclearity, unitality or simplicity. For exact algebras, it proves that the fixed-amplification property already makes every positive element properly infinite[2]. Exact algebras are a large, well-behaved class defined through tensor products. So all three notions agree for exact algebras[3]. Combined with earlier results of Kirchberg and Rørdam, every separable nuclear algebra with the fixed-amplification property absorbs O∞[4]. Absorbing O∞ means A ⊗ O∞ is again A, where O∞ is generated by infinitely many isometries like S1 and S2.

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has formal statements of the two main theorems. They are the ordinary-to-strong implication and the fixed-amplification result for exact algebras. So the paper proves both, as far as the Lean statements match the paper. The O∞ absorption step uses earlier published results. No specialist review is published.
hypeCheck: A solid answer to a listed question, with Lean checks of both main theorems. The weak-to-ordinary step for nonexact algebras stays open. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A family of operators on a Hilbert space closed under sums, products, adjoints and limits.
A way to say one positive element fits below another, by squeezing it with operators up to small errors.
A positive element h with h ⊕ h fitting below h in Cuntz comparison.
Every positive element of the algebra is properly infinite.
Any two positive elements can be cut apart at once, with their mixed entry made arbitrarily small.
An algebra whose minimal tensor product preserves short exact sequences; a large, well-behaved class.
The C*-algebra generated by infinitely many isometries with mutually orthogonal ranges.
An operator that keeps the length of every vector.
